GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Watch a point that stays put while the rest of the picture bends around it.
How to play: Drag the dots A, B or D; D slides along the upright line. Drag D first to unlock the Premise and Proof switches, and press Reset to start over.
Look for the math

The picture behaves like a hinge. As D slides along the line through the middle of AB, both little triangles swing and the diamond between them changes shape. Yet the corner marked C never moves at all.

Two triangles that turn by a third of a turn

AB is fixed. D may move anywhere on the perpendicular bisector of AB, so AD and BD are always equal. On those two sides we build equilateral triangles: turn AD by 60° about A to find F, and turn BD by 60° about B to find E. Since D is on the bisector, F and E are mirror images in it, and the line FE is parallel to AB.

The rhombus is really a reflection

C is chosen so that DFCE is a rhombus. The diagonals of a rhombus cross at their midpoints and at right angles, so C is just the reflection of D in the line FE. Tick Premise to see that line and the equal-length marks. The cut-the-knot page adds that the small triangles need not be built outside ABD: if both are built inside instead, the conclusion is still true. That is exactly what happens when D crosses to the other side of AB.

Why C cannot move

Let M be the midpoint of AB, s the length of AB, n the unit direction from M towards D, and h how far D sits from M along n. The 60° turns put F and E at height h/2 − √3·s/2 along n. Reflecting D in FE changes its height to twice that, minus h:

2(h/2 − √3·s/2) − h = −√3·s/2

The height h cancels, so C is always M − (√3/2)·s·n. That is one of the two points which make ABC equilateral: its distance to both A and B is s. This is the old construction of an equilateral triangle with a rusty compass. The logic test confirms the claim on a grid of bases and many heights of D, on both sides of AB, and compares every picture with a second transcription of the Java applet's own rotate, intersect and reflect methods. One small change from the Java: it snapped D onto the bisector only while D was being dragged, whereas this page keeps D on the line at all times, as the puzzle states.

Drag D across AB: the little triangles flip from outside to inside, but C does not budge. Then tick Proof to see the five equal circles behind the construction.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
